science.title: Psychological capital links social support to student outcomes in both economically disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged college students
science.description: Drawing on social support theory, positive psychology, and resource-based perspectives, this study examined whether psychological capital (PsyCap) mediates the relationships among teacher support, peer support, and family cohesion and two student outcomes—meaning in life and learning engagement—as well as whether these mediating pathways differ between economically disadvantaged and economically non-disadvantaged college students. Data were collected through an online survey from 1756 students, of whom 646 were disadvantaged and 1110 non-disadvantaged, studying at a university in southern China. Structural equation modeling and multi-group analysis showed that PsyCap mediated several pathways linking social support and family cohesion to student outcomes, although the significance and magnitude of these indirect effects varied across economic groups. These findings highlight the role of PsyCap as a protective psychological resource, particularly for economically disadvantaged students, and provide practical implications for designing targeted interventions to strengthen student well-being and learning engagement.

science.title: Fossil shark scales reveal how ocean productivity shapes shark populations
science.description:
Long before intensive human fishing began, Pacific reefs naturally supported far more sharks than Caribbean reefs, according to a new study. The findings, based on an analysis of fossilized shark scales, suggest that differences in ocean productivity – and not fishing alone – have shaped shark populations for thousands of years, information that could guide future conservation efforts. Shark populations have declined worldwide, especially on coral reefs, where many species are now at high risk of extinction. However, conservation efforts have been hindered by a lack of historical baselines showing what healthy shark populations looked like before widespread human impacts, making it difficult to set realistic conservation and recovery goals. To address this gap, Erin Dillon and colleagues reconstructed reef shark communities spanning the past 7,000 years by analyzing fossilized shark dermal denticles – tiny tooth-like scales preserved in coral reef sediments. Denticle abundance in reef sediments closely reflects shark populations.
 
Dillon et al. collected fossil denticles from the Caribbean and Pacific coasts of Panama, two neighboring regions with contrasting ocean conditions and levels of human activity but many of the same shark species. By comparing ancient (~7 to 3 ka) and recent (past ~100 years) sediments, the authors were able to determine natural baselines for reef shark populations and evaluate how environmental conditions and human pressures have shaped their decline over time. The findings revealed that healthy reef shark populations naturally differed between Pacific and Caribbean reefs. Pacific reefs supported about 20 times more sharks than Caribbean reefs thousands of years before intensive fishing. Since then, Caribbean shark populations, particularly fast-swimming pelagic species, have declined by roughly 75%, while Pacific populations have remained comparatively stable, despite experiencing higher historical fishing pressure.  As a result, the gap between the two regions has widened dramatically, with modern Pacific reefs now supporting about 100 times more sharks than comparable Caribbean reefs. Dillon et al. conclude that differences in ocean productivity have long played a crucial role in determining how many sharks a reef can naturally support. The Pacific coast of Panama, fueled by nutrient-rich seasonal upwelling, has historically sustained much larger shark populations and appears more resilient to human impacts than the less productive Caribbean, where shark populations have declined far more dramatically. These findings suggest that conservation goals should be tailored to regional ecological conditions rather than applying a single baseline across different ecosystems. In a related Perspective, Peter Roopnarine discusses the study in greater detail.

science.title: Interaction-limited conductivity of twisted bilayer graphene revealed by giant terahertz photoresistance
science.description: Identifying the microscopic processes limiting conductivity is essential for understanding correlated quantum materials. In twisted bilayer graphene, metallic resistivity follows ρ ~ Tα with widely varying α, fueling competing interpretations from phonon-limited transport and umklapp scattering to strange metallicity and heavy-fermion renormalization. Here, we use terahertz excitation to selectively heat electrons while keeping the lattice cold, separating electron-electron from electron-phonon contributions to resistivity. We observe a giant terahertz photoresistance — reaching several kΩ — showing that electron-electron scattering remains significant even in regimes previously attributed to phonons, including the linear-in-T resistivity near the magic angle. Away from it, photoresistance coexists with quadratic-in-T resistivity at low carrier densities where umklapp and Baber scattering are kinematically forbidden. We identify the breakdown of Galilean invariance in the Dirac dispersion, enabling inter-valley electron-electron collisions, as a possible origin. Our approach establishes terahertz-driven hot-electron transport as a framework for disentangling scattering mechanisms in low-density quantum materials. Electron-phonon and electron-electron scattering can contribute to linear-in-temperature resistivity in materials. Here, the authors use terahertz excitation to separate electronic and phonon contributions to the resistivity and reveal interaction-limited conductivity in twisted bilayer graphene.

science.title: Handgrip strength is not independently associated with steatosis in people with MASLD
science.description: Reduced handgrip strength (HGS) is considered a surrogate marker of whole-body muscle strength and has been associated with sarcopenia and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). This cross-sectional study investigated the relationship between HGS, steatosis and fibrosis in a primary care and endocrinology cohort. Steatosis was defined as a controlled attenuation parameter (CAP™) > 248 dB/m, and fibrosis as vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE™) > 8 kPa. HGS was measured using a hydraulic hand dynamometer and expressed as absolute HGS, BMI-adjusted HGS (bHGS), and height-adjusted HGS (hHGS). Among 422 participants (median age 61 years; median BMI 28.1 kg/m2), 264 (62.5%) had MASLD and 57 (13.5%) had fibrosis. Participants with MASLD had significantly lower bHGS than those without MASLD, whereas absolute HGS and hHGS did not differ. In the MASLD cohort, bHGS showed a weak inverse correlation with CAP. However, after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, no independent associations were observed between any of the HGS measures and steatosis. These findings suggest that reduced bHGS, but not hHGS or absolute HGS, is associated with greater steatosis severity but is not an independent predictor of MASLD or liver fibrosis.

science.title: Health-related fitness mediates the longitudinal association between engagement in fundamental movement skill-related activities and social interaction abilities in the ABCD study
science.description: Under the Know it-Do it-Love it (KDL) framework, structured physical activity is expected to support adolescents’ social development. Guided by the KDL concept, this study examined the longitudinal association between engagement in fundamental movement skill (FMS)-related activities and adolescents’ social interaction abilities, as well as the mediating role of health-related fitness, using the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) dataset. Using data from the ABCD Study 3.0 (N = 4950 adolescents aged 9–11 years, 2-year follow-up), social interaction abilities were assessed using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Latent Class Growth Analysis identified four trajectories: improvement (8.7%), sustained high (5.4%), decline (10.8%), and sustained low (75.1%). Given the large-scale nature of the ABCD dataset and the absence of direct FMS assessments, this study operationalized FMS-related activity engagement through structured sports participation time as a developmentally appropriate proxy. Participation time in ’social-type’ sports (e.g., soccer, basketball) was used as a proxy for engagement in structured, socially interactive FMS-related activities. Participation time in ’individual-type’ sports (e.g., swimming, running) was used as a proxy for individually oriented FMS-related activity engagement. These sport-participation variables should be interpreted as proxies for FMS-related activity engagement rather than as direct assessments of locomotor or object-control skill proficiency. Correlation, regression, and structural equation modeling (SEM) were used to examine predictive and mediating relationships. FMS proxy variables were positively correlated with social interaction abilities (r = 0.359, $$p < 0.001$$), with locomotor proxies showing the strongest association (r = 0.381, $$p < 0.001$$). Regression analysis indicated that locomotor proxies significantly predicted follow-up social interaction abilities after adjusting for baseline social interaction ability ($$\beta $$ = 0.213, $$p < 0.001$$), whereas object-control proxies were not significant. SEM results showed a non-significant direct effect of FMS proxies (B = 0.07, p = 0.48), but a significant indirect effect through health-related fitness (B = 0.10, 95% CI 0.03–0.18), accounting for 58.8% of the total effect. Engagement in FMS-related activities was longitudinally associated with adolescents’ social interaction development in part through health-related fitness, especially endurance and muscular strength, rather than through direct behavioral pathways alone. These findings provide observational support for the pathways proposed in the KDL concept.
